opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. If you spend any time online now, you can almost instantly spot an AI-generated image. There's a certain glossiness to it: overly smooth skin, very saturated colors, dramatic lighting that looks like a perfect golden hour, everything centered and symmetrical, a kind of hyper-polished stock-photo aesthetic. People have started calling it "AI slop," and that recognizability has become a real problem.

Part of it comes from how these models are trained and tuned. In the pretraining phase you learn from a huge, diverse distribution of images, but then there's post-training: aesthetic fine-tuning, preference optimization, reward models. When you optimize for what raters say looks "good" or "beautiful," you push the model toward a narrow mode. Each individual image looks appealing in isolation, but collectively they converge on the same look. You trade diversity and realism for a kind of averaged-out prettiness.

That matters for a few reasons. For creative professionals, if everything the model makes has the same signature, it's much less useful as a tool. A photographer or designer wants a specific look, maybe a gritty, candid, slightly imperfect snapshot, and the model keeps pulling them back toward this polished default. It limits creative control.

There's also a realism issue. Real photographs are messy. They have sensor noise, odd framing, imperfect lighting, people who aren't perfectly posed. If the goal is a model that can genuinely depict the world, that idealized style is a failure mode, even if it scores well on some aesthetic benchmarks.

And there's a perception problem. Once audiences associate that look with low-effort generated content, anything with it gets dismissed, regardless of the intent or quality behind it. So the challenge for those of us building these models is figuring out how to keep the quality and prompt adherence gains from post-training without collapsing onto one aesthetic: preserving diversity, giving users real stylistic control, and making the default output feel more natural and less like it came from a machine.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training preferences and aesthetic tuning push outputs toward a narrow style, but it does not attribute that style to early efforts to narrow outputs to images the models could generate well.

r002.rationale: It says the recognizable look is easy to spot online and that audiences associate it with low-effort generated content, causing images with that look to be dismissed.

r003.rationale: The response supports broader stylistic variety and user control, but does not describe a shift from audiences being impressed by AI-looking images to expecting a broader range.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really interesting phenomenon, and it's something we've been thinking about a lot. If you look at the images coming out of most of the big models over the last couple of years, you can often tell at a glance that they're AI generated, even before you notice any specific artifact. There's a certain quality to them. The lighting is very dramatic, everything is kind of glossy and over-saturated, skin is too smooth, the compositions are very centered and symmetrical. It's almost like every image has been through the same Instagram filter, and people have started calling it the "AI look" or the "AI aesthetic."

And I think the reason it's become a problem is twofold. One is just that it's become a bit of a tell. People have learned to recognize it, and once you recognize it, it starts to feel cheap. It's a little like the uncanny valley, but for style rather than realism. If I'm a designer or an artist and I generate something and it immediately reads as "oh, that's AI," that undermines what I'm trying to do. I want the image to look like what I asked for, not like what the model prefers.

The second thing, and this is the part I find more interesting from a research perspective, is that it's a symptom of something deeper about how these models are trained. A lot of it comes from preference tuning. When you take a base model and then you fine-tune it on human preference data, you're pushing the model toward whatever people click on in a side-by-side comparison. And in a quick A/B test, people tend to pick the image that's more vivid, more contrasty, more polished. So the model learns that's what "good" means, and it collapses toward that one mode. You lose a lot of the diversity that was actually in the training data. Real photographs are often kind of boring. They're flat, the lighting is bad, the framing is a little off. And that's exactly what gets optimized away.

So the model becomes really good at producing one very specific kind of image, and really bad at producing the full range of what visual content actually looks like. If you ask for a casual snapshot or something that looks like it was shot on a phone, it struggles, because it's been trained to always make things look like a stock photo or a movie poster. And for a lot of real use cases, that's not what people want. They want control. They want the output to match their intent, whether that's cinematic or mundane.

So when we talk about the AI look being a problem, I'd say it's really about mode collapse and loss of controllability, and those are things you have to think about pretty carefully in the training pipeline rather than just bolting on fixes afterward.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the aesthetic to preference tuning that favors vivid, polished images and reduces diversity, but does not attribute it to early efforts to narrow outputs to images the models could generate well.

r002.rationale: It says people recognize the aesthetic and that it can feel cheap, but does not clearly say audience saturation with it has made it less appealing.

r003.rationale: The response says people want control and a broader range of outputs, but does not describe a shift from being impressed by AI-looking images to expecting broader imagery.

astra-6.text:
I think the problem is that generating a beautiful image isn’t necessarily the same as generating the image somebody wants. A recognizable AI look might be appealing initially, but if everything has that same lighting, that same polish, it starts to feel repetitive. And you lose a lot of the variety that makes images interesting in the first place.

It also becomes a question of control. If you ask for something mundane—a casual snapshot, for example—and the model keeps turning it into this highly produced image, then its default aesthetic is getting in the way of your intent. Ideally, that polished look should be one option you can choose, rather than something you have to fight to get away from.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute the recognizable aesthetic to early efforts to narrow the output distribution.

r002.rationale: It says a repeated look can feel repetitive, but does not state that audience saturation has made the aesthetic less appealing.

r003.rationale: It values variety and user control, but does not describe a shift from audiences being impressed by AI-looking images to expecting broader imagery.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the problem is that when you ask for an image, you usually want the model to follow your intent, and that includes how the image looks. But a lot of these models have a very strong default aesthetic—everything is a little too polished, the lighting is dramatic, the skin is very smooth. Even when the content is different, the images start to feel the same.

That can be appealing initially, but it becomes a limitation if you're trying to make something that feels specific or personal. You don't necessarily want someone’s first reaction to be, “Oh, that’s an AI image.” You want them to engage with what you’re trying to communicate. So the challenge is giving people more control over the aesthetic, rather than having the model’s default style dominate the result.

r001.rationale: The response describes a strong default aesthetic but does not attribute it to early efforts to narrow the output distribution to images models could generate well.

r002.rationale: It says the look can be appealing initially and later limiting, but does not say audience saturation has made it less appealing.

r003.rationale: It calls for more aesthetic control and specific or personal images, but does not state that audience expectations shifted from being impressed by AI-looking images to expecting broader imagery.
